extracted.intended_audience: readers of political economy, economists, and educated public interested in classical economic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition (Adam Smith) on how the supply, consumption, and taxation of gold and silver affect prices, wages, and international trade; includes a classification of types of rude produce and their price behavior under improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative advancement of newly discovered countries
rubrics_metrics.description: Newly discovered countries (e.g., Peru, Mexico) were in many arts, agriculture, and commerce much more ignorant than commonly represented; commerce was largely barter with scarce division of labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence: lack of coined money, artisans maintained by sovereign/nobles/priests, little manufacture exported to Europe; Spanish conquerors had difficulty procuring subsistence, suggesting the reports of populousness and high cultivation are largely fabulous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of abundant fertile land in colonies
rubrics_metrics.description: In new colonies, fertile soil and cheapness of land compensate many defects in civil government, promoting rapid advancement in agriculture, improvement, and population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: reported increases in Lima's population (Frezier vs Ulloa) marking rapid growth; America as a growing market for silver-driven produce with demand increasing faster than in Europe.

rubrics_metrics.name: American silver as an engine of intercontinental commerce
rubrics_metrics.description: Silver from the New World is one of the principal commodities by which commerce between distant parts of the old world is carried on, connecting Europe with the East Indies and China.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanisms: direct Acapulco-Manila trade, indirect European trade; silver often carried from Europe to India because it purchases comparatively more labour and commodities there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative value of precious metals across regions
rubrics_metrics.description: The proportion between gold and silver varies by region and over time (e.g., Europe historically 1:10–12, later 1:14–15; China ~1:10–12; Japan ~1:8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These differences explain why silver is often more advantageous to carry to India and China; example: in China 10–12 oz silver buys 1 oz gold, while in Europe 14–15 oz silver is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Money price differences driven by abundance of food and labour productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: In rice countries (China, Indostan) with multiple abundant harvests, the abundance of food lowers the money price of labour and the money price of manufactures relative to Europe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: richer classes can command larger retinues; wages purchase less food (real wage lower), and nominal prices of manufactures are lower; inland navigation reduces transport costs, further lowering prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Durability of metals causing price steadiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Because metals are durable and remain in use for long periods, the price of metals varies less year-to-year than that of perishable produce (like corn).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: corn consumed within a year vs iron or gold that can remain in use for decades or millennia; hence annual variations in mine output affect metal prices less than crop output affects corn prices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual consumption factors for precious metals
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual supply from mines must cover not only the increase of coin/plate in growing economies but also continual consumption through wearing, cleaning, certain manufactures, transport losses, and concealment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Birmingham's annual use of gold/silver in gilding/plating (~£50,000) shows rapid consumption in particular manufactures; treasures buried and knowledge lost also remove metal from circulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical estimates of annual importation into Spain/Portugal
rubrics_metrics.description: Contemporary manuscript and printed accounts (Meggens; other authors) estimate annual registered importation of gold and silver into Spain and Portugal at about six million sterling (with some estimates up to ~£6,075,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accounts include registered imports, smuggled quantities estimates, and tax-based inferences (e.g., Portuguese tax on Brazilian gold). These figures inform arguments about supply relative to consumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity in market vs relative value distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: The ordinary proportion between values of two commodities is not necessarily the same as the proportion between their quantities in the market; a cheap commodity may exist in greater quantity and total value than a dear one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one ox priced at ten guineas is not evidence there are few oxen relative to lambs priced at 3s.6d; similarly, silver's larger market quantity relative to gold does not imply its value ratio equals the quantity ratio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taxation's effect on metal prices and mining profitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Different taxes on gold and silver (e.g., Spanish tax: gold 1/20, silver 1/10; Portuguese gold tax 1/5 in Brazil historically) affect how near the market price is to the lowest remunerative price and thus influence mining activity and supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reductions in tax can make previously unprofitable mines workable, increasing supply and retarding price rises; conversely, high taxes can limit supply and push prices up nearer to the lowest economic limit of production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Growing scarcity of mines and three compensatory events
rubrics_metrics.description: As mines become more expensive to work (greater depths, pumping, ventilation), this 'growing scarcity' must be compensated by either: (1) a proportionate increase in the metal's price; (2) a proportionate diminution of the tax upon the metal; or (3) partly by each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical analogy: gold rose relative to silver despite tax reduction on gold; similar dynamics could make silver rise in price despite tax reductions. Successive tax reductions may delay but not prevent price rises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dynamic equilibrium between importation and consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: There will be a period when annual consumption equals annual importation; as the mass of metals increases, consumption rises faster than mass, reducing value until equilibrium; if importation later diminishes, mass may fall and value rise until new balance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mass of metals in circulation affects consumption rates (more mass => more usage and less care), so long-term trends in importation and consumption determine metal values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for suspecting continued decrease in silver's value
rubrics_metrics.description: Observed increases in Europe's wealth and rising nominal prices of many rude produce may lead many to believe silver's value continues to fall; however, Smith argues wealth increases do not necessarily make silver cheaper in real terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wealth attracts precious metals because they command higher prices there, not because they are cheaper; rising nominal prices of non-corn produce may reflect those commodities becoming really dearer, not silver becoming cheaper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of rude produce into three sorts and their price behavior under improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Rude produce divides into: (1) things scarce to multiply by human industry (e.g., rare birds/fish) whose real price can rise without bound; (2) things human industry can multiply in proportion to demand, whose price has an upper boundary; (3) things where industry’s efficacy is limited or uncertain, whose price may fall, remain same, or rise depending on accidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First sort: luxury rarities rise enormously as wealth increases (example: woodcocks selling for twenty guineas), independent of silver's value. Second sort: supply can meet demand to some limit. Third sort: outcomes depend on success of industrial effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: First sort examples and explanatory note
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of the first sort (hard-to-multiply commodities): rare and singular birds and fishes, many sorts of game, wild-fowl, birds of passage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because human industry cannot substantially increase supply, rising demand due to wealth can increase their prices to extreme levels; historical Roman prices for rarities are explained by this mechanism rather than a low value of silver.
